accuracy_findings.claim: A building can be damaged when a Navarch's conquest, bombardment or pillage resolves. ... See [[siege]] for which buildings can be hit.
accuracy_findings.problem: Brief item 1 includes a plain-text pointer, "how many per result: plain text, Navarchs". The page never says that the number of buildings hit depends on the attack's result. That leaves out a fact players get wrong: a failed conquest or bombardment can still damage buildings. A reader could take "when it resolves" to mean "when it succeeds".
accuracy_findings.evidence: conquest.ex:122-128 damaged_buildings_count: critical_failure 0, normal_failure 2, normal_success 6, critical_success 2. raid.ex:100-106: 0, 1, 5, 6. loot.ex:101-107: 0, 0, 2, 1. The count reaches StellarSystem.raid/4 through {:release_siege, _, damaged_buildings_count, result} (conquest.ex:140, raid.ex:117, loot.ex:118), and apply_building_damage runs it whatever the result (stellar_system.ex:319-320, 1695-1701).
accuracy_findings.fix: Add one plain-text clause after the first sentence, for example: "How many depends on the attack's result, and even a failed conquest or bombardment can damage some." Keep the Navarchs chapter as plain text and add no numbers, since attack results belong to Navarchs.

clarity_findings.claim: The 'A damaged building:' bullet list breaks its own parallel grammar on the last item.
clarity_findings.problem: The first five bullets all read as predicates of the damaged building itself ('Gives none of its bonuses…', 'Still mobilizes its workforce.', 'Still counts as the one copy…', 'Cannot be upgraded…', 'Can still be destroyed…'), but the sixth switches subject to 'the system' ('If it is a shipyard, the system cannot order its ships.'). A reader scanning the list for what the building still does or doesn't do hits an unexpected subject change on the last line.
clarity_findings.fix: Rephrase the last bullet to keep the building as the implied subject, e.g. 'Blocks the system's ship orders, if it is a shipyard.' to match the voice of the other five bullets.

clarity_findings.claim: The repair-cost example doesn't actually demonstrate the rounding it announces.
clarity_findings.problem: The sentence right after the example block says 'Both costs are rounded to the nearest whole number,' but the two example lines (8,000 × 0.5 = 4,000 and 1,000 × 0.5 = 500) both divide evenly, so the reader never sees a case where rounding changes anything — the claim has to be taken on faith rather than shown.
clarity_findings.fix: Swap one example figure for a number that doesn't divide evenly by the factor (e.g. 8,050 credits or 1,050 production) so the rounded result is visibly different from the raw product.

votes.reason: Well-organized with clear headers, a worked-number example, and a screenshot whose two highlight boxes line up exactly with the callouts in the caption ("A damaged building (1) and its Repair button (2)") — reads clean in one pass with only small stumbles.
stumbles: The screenshot has several other icons (a flagged tile badge "2", an up-arrow/person tile badge "1", gear and horseshoe icons) that sit right next to the two highlighted marks but are never explained on this page, so a first glance briefly wonders which icons matter
"Still mobilizes its workforce" is dropped in as a bare fact with no reason given for why that matters if the building is already producing nothing

"0.5 times the credit and production of the building's current level" briefly leaves open whether 'current level' means something special for a never-upgraded (level 1) building until the worked example underneath resolves it

votes.reason: Every rule (what causes damage, what a damaged building can/can't do, exact repair cost formula with a worked example, cancellation, and siege lockout) is stated once, plainly, and the screenshot's two highlighted callouts (damaged building icon, Repair button) match the caption text directly.
stumbles: Minor only: the worked example ('8,000 credits × 0.5 = 4,000 credits') uses arbitrary numbers not tied to any specific building level, so a reader briefly has to recognize it's illustrative rather than a real building's cost.

Minor only: figure caption reads 'A damaged building (1) and its Repair button (2)' but on screen the Repair button (mark 2) sits above the damaged-building icon (mark 1), a slight mismatch between caption order and visual order.
